title: The encoding is the claim
objective: Re-encode the transfer in 64-bit integers, then say why the guarded sender holds only with a positive amount, why the recipient wraps, and how a guard that mixes signed and unsigned comparisons lets the overdraft back in.

blocks.md: A solver's answer is about the encoding you gave it, and the encoding is a choice. So far the balances were mathematical integers. Real code stores them in 64 bits. Two questions before the lesson starts; guess if you are not sure.

choice.prompt: A claim proved over `Int`, "the guarded transfer never overdraws the sender", moves to code that stores balances as 64-bit integers. What carries over?

options.text: All of it: the guard did not change, so neither does the proof.
options.why: `Int` never overflows, and 64-bit integers do. The encoding changed even though the guard did not.

options.text: Half of it: the sender's side when `amount > 0`, not the recipient's.
options.why: Over 64 bits the guarded sender still has no overdraft when the amount is positive, and the recipient's credit can wrap {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}.

options.text: Nothing: 64-bit arithmetic can wrap in any operation.
options.why: Overflow happens in particular operations. The sender's subtraction stays in range under the guard.

choice.prompt: On Z3 bit-vectors, is `<` signed or unsigned?

options.why: The Z3 guide's "Machine Arithmetic" says so. `ULT` is the unsigned comparison.
The unsigned comparisons have their own names, such as `ULT` and `ULE`.

options.text: It depends on how the variable was declared.
options.why: Bit-vectors carry no sign. Each operator chooses one.

blocks.md: Over `Int`, a balance never overflows. The 64-bit encoding is `BitVec(64)`: its `<`, `<=` and `-` are signed, and its arithmetic wraps around at 2⁶⁴. Take the guard `X <= A` and leave out the premise `X > 0`. Then ask whether the sender can end below zero.

blocks.direction: Query asserts: 64-bit balances and an amount that pass the guard, with no requirement that the amount be positive, and a sender who ends below zero. `sat` means one exists.

code.text:
from z3 import *
A, B, X = BitVecs('A B X', 64)      # 64-bit balances and amount
s = Solver()
s.add(A >= 0, B >= 0, X <= A)       # the guard, with no X > 0
s.add(A - X < 0)                    # the sender ends below zero
print(s.check())
print(s.model())

tap.property: the sender never ends below zero

options.why: A negative amount turns `A - X` into an addition, and the sum can wrap past the largest 64-bit value {{run:RUN-z3-bv64-negamt}}.
Over `Int`, a negative amount makes the sender richer, never poorer. At 64 bits, subtracting a negative amount is an addition that can overflow.
Bit-vector queries like this one are decided.

blocks.after:
Z3 found a transfer {{run:RUN-z3-bv64-negamt}}. It prints bit-vector values as unsigned numbers. In the recorded model X is 9223372036854775809, which a signed 64-bit integer reads as -9223372036854775807: a negative amount. Add `X > 0` and the same search has no model {{run:RUN-z3-bv64-negamt}}.

Zero and negative amounts are a decision, not a detail. Stage S3 records it.

choice.prompt: A pull request guards the transfer with `X <= A + 1`. The premises are `A >= 0` and `X > 0`. Which values are a witness that the sender can end below zero? Pick small values and treat the arithmetic as 64-bit.

options.why: The guard passes, because 6 is at most 5 + 1, and the sender ends at -1.
The sender ends at 0, which is not below zero.
7 is above 5 + 1, so the guard rejects this transfer.
The premise `X > 0` fails. A negative amount is a different bug, and it is not an allowed input here.

blocks.md: Conservation over 64 bits is the next question. Subtracting from one balance and adding to the other wrap in opposite ways, so the total may still hold.

blocks.direction: Query asserts: whatever leaves the sender arrives at the recipient, with every operation wrapping at 2⁶⁴. `prove` prints `proved` when no counterexample exists.

code.text:
from z3 import *
A, B, X = BitVecs('A B X', 64)
prove((A - X) + (B + X) == A + B)   # conservation, modulo 2**64

options.why: Arithmetic modulo 2⁶⁴ still cancels, so a wrap moves no money in this sum {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}.
A wrap changes a balance, but the two wraps cancel in the total.
Bit-vector arithmetic is decided.

blocks.after:
Conservation still holds {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}, and the guarded sender still has no overdraft when the amount is positive {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}. The recipient is another matter. In the recorded model, B is 9223372036850581504 and X is 4194304. Their sum is 2⁶³, which signed 64-bit reads as -2⁶³, so the recipient ends below zero {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}.

A related query gave a different witness {{run:RUN-z3-bv64-pyodide}}. Witnesses are not canonical, so graded items check the property, never the values.

blocks.md: The guard protects the sender, not the recipient. It bounds the debit and never looks at the credit.

choice.prompt: Which statement about the 64-bit version of your claim is true?

options.text: The `Int` claim carries over to `i64` code unchanged, with no new encoding.
options.why: `Int` never overflows, and `i64` does, so the claim needs its own encoding.

options.text: The claim covers the recipient's balance too, since the same guard bounds the credit.
options.why: The recipient's credit can wrap, and the guard never bounds it {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}.

options.text: On an overflowing credit, PostgreSQL `bigint` ends in the same state as the 64-bit model.
options.why: PostgreSQL raises error 22003 and the balance keeps its old value, so the database refuses a step the model takes {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}.

options.text: Given `amount > 0`, the guarded sender stays at zero or above and the total is conserved modulo 2⁶⁴.
options.why: Both hold over 64 bits {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}. That is what the claim covers, and nothing more.

segments.title: Two readings of the same bits

blocks.md: A bit-vector has no sign of its own. Each operator reads the bits one way: `<`, `<=` and `-` are signed, and `ULT`, `ULE` and `UGT` are unsigned. A guard and a property that read the same bits differently disagree about the state.

blocks.direction: Query asserts: a guard written with unsigned comparisons, and a sender who ends below zero when read as signed. `sat` means one exists.

code.text:
from z3 import *
A, X = BitVecs('A X', 64)
s = Solver()
s.add(UGT(X, 0), ULE(X, A))         # the guard reads the bits as unsigned
s.add(A - X < 0)                    # the property reads them as signed
print(s.check())
print(s.model())

tap.property: the sender never ends below zero

options.why: A has its top bit set. The unsigned guard sees a huge balance, and the signed property sees a negative one {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}.
The guard and the property read the same bits, but not the same way, so they disagree about the state.
Bit-vector queries like this one are decided.

blocks.after: Z3 found a state {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}. Pick one reading of the bits and use it in every comparison.

blocks.md:
Here is what "64-bit" means across the tools you will meet.

| Semantics | An overflowing credit | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Lean `Int` | cannot overflow: arbitrary precision | the definition of the type |
| Z3 `Int` | cannot overflow: mathematical integers | the definition, and the Z3 guide's "Arithmetic" |
| Z3 BitVec 64 | wraps modulo 2⁶⁴, and signedness is per operator | {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}} |
| PostgreSQL `bigint` | raises error 22003, and the balance keeps its old value | {{run:RUN-pg-claims}} |
| PostgreSQL `numeric` | raises at its declared bound | {{run:RUN-pg-numeric-bound}} |
| Rust `i64` | a debug build panics, a release build wraps, and `checked_add` returns `None` | {{run:RUN-rust-i64}} |

Stage S6 comes back to the PostgreSQL row. There, your model takes a step the database refuses.

Two dated incidents sit in the specimen cabinet's "dated incidents" filter, as toy models you can run. In 2010, Bitcoin's check on a transaction's outputs passed when they overflowed in the sum, and the transaction created value {{run:RUN-z3-btc2010}}. In 2006, Joshua Bloch described a binary-search midpoint, `(low + high) / 2`, that leaves its interval when `low + high` overflows a 32-bit integer {{run:RUN-z3-bloch06}}.

choice.prompt: A guard reads `ULE(X, A)` and the property reads `A - X < 0`. Z3 finds a witness whose `A` has its top bit set. Which kind of bug is it?

options.text: A signedness mismatch: the guard and the property read the bits differently.
options.why: The unsigned guard accepts the transfer, and the signed property sees a negative balance.

options.text: Overflow on the credit: the recipient's sum wraps past the top of the range.
options.why: The recipient does not appear in this query, so no credit is involved.

options.text: A negative amount: the sender is asked to send less than nothing at all.
options.why: The guard `UGT(X, 0)` is about the amount, but the witness's amount is positive. The trouble is in how `A` is read.

choice.prompt: A guarded transfer with `amount > 0` is encoded over `Int` and again over 64-bit integers. The violation is that the recipient ends below zero. What will Z3 return for each encoding?

options.why: The 64-bit credit can wrap, which an `Int` credit cannot.
Over `Int` the recipient only gains. Over 64 bits the credit can wrap negative {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}.
With `amount > 0` and `b >= 0`, an `Int` recipient cannot end below zero.
Bit-vector queries like this one are decided.

choice.prompt: Balances are signed 8-bit integers, from -128 to 127. The guard is `X <= A`, with `A >= 0`, `B >= 0` and `X > 0`. Which values make the recipient wrap?

options.why: The recipient ends at 70, which fits in 8 bits, so nothing wraps.
The recipient would wrap, but the guard rejects this transfer because 100 is above 50.
The guard passes, and 100 + 50 is 150, which wraps to -106 in 8 bits.
The recipient ends at 125, which is just inside the range. This is near the edge, not over it.

blocks.md: Your second claim card is CL-1.5: under signed 64-bit integers with `amount > 0`, the guarded sender cannot go below zero. Its stamp says the recipient is not covered.

blocks.md: The concepts page says a VALID result "covers only the parts of the input captured through policy variables in the translated premises and claims" (read 2026-10-23). What the checker never saw, it never checked. Here the unseen part was the width of an integer.

blocks.md: Revise the limitations in your README: name the encoding, and add the recipient as not covered. Then predict the encoding mutation in Prove-it.

The server ran in postgres:18@sha256:74935e72241653ca55e0414067e6d8763aceb8a810eb51b452253ec3dcfc4336 (the digest RUN-scaffold pins) with --network none and --memory=6g and trust authentication, and was removed when the script finished. argv lists the three commands in order: the server's start, psql through docker exec and sh, and the removal; the exit code is psql's. Between the start and psql the recorder waited until docker logs w1t12-pg showed "PostgreSQL init process complete" and "database system is ready to accept connections" at least twice (the image's entrypoint first runs a temporary server for its initialization, which prints the first of them) and docker exec w1t12-pg pg_isready -U postgres exited 0, polling at most 120 times with a 0.5 s pause between polls; a psql started straight after the start finds no server socket and exits 2. psql's stdout and stderr were merged inside the container by 2>&1, so the log's lines are in the order psql wrote them (docker exec without a terminal carries the two streams apart, and its CLI prints them in no fixed order); the check psql-order fails a log in which an ERROR line comes after the sqlstate or balance echo that follows its statement.

LAST_ERROR_SQLSTATE keeps its value after a later success in psql, so the script echoes it only after a statement that failed.

RUN-rust-i64.title: Rust 1.96.0 i64: the dev profile panics on overflow, the release profile wraps, and checked_add returns None
verdict_lines: note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
b + x = -9223372036854775808 (wrapped; non-negativity broken; i128 total changed by -18446744073709551616)

stdout: b + x = -9223372036854775808 (wrapped; non-negativity broken; i128 total changed by -18446744073709551616)

notes: Recorded by W1-T12. values.debug and values.release hold what each binary did: debug.panicked and debug.panic_message (the dev profile's overflow check fired inside the source's catch_unwind), release.wrapped and release.b_plus_x (the release profile wrapped), and checked_add in both. Cite one as {{run:RUN-rust-i64#values.release.b_plus_x}}.

The crate is byte-identical to research/evidence/a2r3/rust (spine section 9.5: its source existed and its output was never committed); `record.mjs check` compares the copies. The program catches its own panic, so both binaries exit 0: the debug build's panic is the message on stderr and the line "b + x panicked (overflow check)" on stdout.

The two `Running` lines in the log show the exact rustc arguments: the dev profile (cargo's default) passes no -C opt-level, and the release profile passes -C opt-level=3. That the dev build checks overflow and the release build wraps is what the two binaries printed; the profile defaults that explain it are cargo's and rustc's documented ones [D]. The log keeps the panic's thread id verbatim (89 in this recording): it is the id of the main thread in the container's process numbering and not part of the result, and no check reads it. The two `Finished` lines carry cargo's own elapsed time, which differs between runs of the same command, so a replay can differ from this log on those lines.
stdout and stderr of each binary are printed in separate sections by rust_i64.sh, so the order of the two streams is never in question.
Placeholder in argv: <sandbox>/crate is a scratch copy of the crate (Cargo.toml and src/main.rs) with rust_i64.sh beside it (the inputs list them); the container sees it as /w.

budget.harness_timeout_s is the wall time after which the recording script would have stopped the docker run (600 s); started_at and duration_s are that docker run's, the container's start and both builds included.
